newsitem.title: INDIA: India seen hurtling towards snap election.
newsitem.headline: India seen hurtling towards snap election.

text.p: A mid-term election in India looks increasingly likely despite attempts by Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's shaky coalition to mend its fractures.

In the latest of its year-long troubles, the 15-party United Front faces tearing itself into pieces over corruption and Hindu nationalism. The coalition's powerful communist partners are pitted against the growing clout of regional allies.

The alliance said on Thursday it had ended a crisis triggered by the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) party which threatened on Monday to pull out of the coalition, citing differences with the communists over how to deal with a corruption scandal.
But the DMK retorted on Friday that the problem had not been solved and would be discussed further at a meeting of the coalition's policymakers on July 25.
Analysts said on Friday that give-and-take seemed to matter little in the alliance because it was perched on a powder-keg of political relationships.
"Any small accident can bring down the government. And accidents you can't predict," political columnist Kewal Varma told Reuters. "It can break any time. Such stresses and strains it cannot absorb."

The centre-left coalition, formed in June 1996 after general elections yielded a hung parliament, compares well with Indian television soap operas in which the same actors appear every day to enact ever-new conflicts.
The regional parties, communists and free-market proponents who banded together last year had one overriding goal -- to keep out the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Instead of consolidating their hold on power, the partners have instead endlessly debated internal differences.
"Nothing positive or cohesive is emerging," Varma said.

Only three months ago, the United Front changed its leader to win back vital parliamentary support from the Congress party, which accused then prime minister H.D. Deve Gowda of not doing enough to stop the BJP.
Opinion polls say the BJP is most likely to gain if there is a snap election.
The BJP controls 193 votes in the 545-member federal parliament. The Congress's 140 deputies support the United Front's 178, again with the sole aim of keeping the BJP at bay.
The latest crisis was sparked when the DMK opposed a bid by the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M) to stop the alliance from admitting a splinter group from Gujral's Janata Dal party.
The splinter group, the Rashtriya Janata Dal, was created because its leader Laloo Prasad Yadav has refused to resign over a corruption scandal.

DMK leaders say that forcing out Yadav's breakaway faction would only hasten a mid-term election. The DMK, which rules the southern state of Tamil Nadu, says it has the support of other regional parties in the alliance.
Yadav, the chief minister of Bihar state in the east, has been indicted by federal police in the $280 million embezzlement scandal but says he is innocent.
The Congress, which has ruled India for all but four years since independence in 1947, is itself raring for a comeback.
"The current fight is between the Congress and the Left (communists), with corruption the issue for the moment," the Asian Age newspaper said in an editorial on Friday.
"The final answer will come from the people as an early election is becoming well nigh inevitable," it said.
DMK leaders say a hard line in ejecting Yadav's group from the coalition can only weaken the coalition's war on the BJP.
"My statement on Monday was aimed at averting a mid-term election," DMK president Muthuvel Karunandhi, who is also the chief minister of Tamil Nadu state, said in Madras on Friday.
The DMK's threat to pull out of the coalition rocked the stock markets. The Bombay 30-share index was at 4,167.24 points on Friday, down from a 33-month high last week of 4,448.06.
Varma said Gujral was clueless in dealing with the crisis.
"Neither has he anything of his own, nor is he a person with imagination who can take risks," he said.
